Chapter One: Looking Beneath the Surface of Everyday Choices
You know, it’s easy to think the world runs on simple, straightforward rules. People work because they want to earn money, crime gets punished, and everyone’s just trying to do the right thing.
But when you look a little closer, you find that the real reasons behind our actions are often hidden—woven together in a mix of incentives, habits, and a bunch of unexpected twists.
The truth is, the world is full of surprises, especially when you start asking the right questions.
Picture this: a city at dusk, streets buzzing with energy. Somewhere, a group of friends is trying to figure out the best way to get home. Some wave down a cab, others start walking, and a few decide to drive. On the surface, these choices seem basic. But underneath, there’s a whole set of calculations—things like cost, convenience, and even whether it’s about to rain.
Most of us don’t even notice how these tiny decisions stack up, or how they’re shaped by forces we rarely think about.
Let’s zoom in on one story. There’s a woman, tired after a long day, standing on a busy street trying to catch a taxi. She’s not the only one—dozens of people are doing the same. Suddenly, it starts to rain. Everything changes. Cabs are suddenly scarce, and drivers seem to disappear into thin air.
It’s not just bad luck—the rain has shifted the whole balance of supply and demand. What seems like a simple ride home quickly turns into a real-life lesson in economics.
And this pattern? You’ll find it everywhere. In hospitals, doctors make choices that can literally mean life or death, but those decisions are often shaped by incentives that have little to do with patient care.
In neighborhoods, people lock their doors and set up alarms to keep out burglars, but sometimes the real risk comes from somewhere they never saw coming. Even the world of crime isn’t always as straightforward as you might think.
Here’s another example: a group of researchers wants to figure out why some neighborhoods feel safer than others. So, they dig through piles of data, searching for clues. You might expect them to find that police presence is the key factor. But what they discover is surprising—sometimes it’s just the way streets are laid out, or how the homes are built. Other times, it’s the quiet influence of social ties, guiding who gets caught and who slips away.
As these stories play out, you start to see that the world is crisscrossed with hidden connections. The choices people make—whether it’s taking a risk, breaking a rule, or helping someone out—are often shaped by incentives nobody else sees.
And here’s the real trick: if you want to understand what’s actually happening, you’ve got to look past the surface and ask yourself, “What’s in it for them?”
This mindset isn’t just for economists or professors. It’s a tool anyone can use, every day, to make sense of what’s happening around them. When you start looking for the hidden incentives behind everyday actions, you’ll start spotting patterns that most people miss.
And once you see those patterns? Trust me—it’s hard to stop.
